content.text:
Operator
At this time, I would like to begin the presentation by turning the call over to Dana's Senior Director of Investor Relations and Corporate Communications, Craig Barber. Please go ahead, Mr. Barber.
Craig Barber
Senior Director of Investor Relations and Corporate Communications, Dana Inc
Good morning and welcome to Dana Incorporated's Q1 2025 Earnings Call. Today's presentation includes forward-looking statements about our expectations for Dana's future performance. Actual results could differ from what we discuss here today. For more details about the factors that could affect future results, please refer to our safe harbor statement found in our public filings and our reports with the SEC. I encourage you to visit our investor website, where you'll find this morning's press release and presentation. As Regina said, the call today is being recorded and supporting materials are the property of Dana Incorporated. They may not be recorded, copied, or rebroadcast without our written consent. With me this morning is Bruce McDonald, Dana Chairman and Chief Executive Officer, and Timothy Kraus, Senior Vice President and Chief Financial Officer. Bruce, now I'll turn the call over to you to get us started.
R. Bruce McDonald
Chairman and CEO, Dana Inc
All right, thank you, Craig, and good morning, everybody. I'll just start with on slide four here in terms of some highlights for Q1. I know there's a lot of interest in the off-highway divestiture process, and we're really not in a position where we can say a lot. You know, what I would tell you is the process continues to be underway. We're pleased with the progress that we've made. It's been competitive, and we have multiple bidders. If you look at Q1, I would say we're pleased with Q1. Our results came in, you know, generally speaking, in line with expectations. I would note that we did have a little bit of a headwind on tariffs of $6 million in Q1.
You know, absent that, we would've had comparable margins to last Q1 despite a pretty big reduction on the top line. Good result there. We see that $6 million coming back. It's just we just couldn't get the paperwork into our customers to get the recovery in the quarter. Really importantly for us, we talked about this on our last earnings call, is we said we're gonna look at our cost reduction plans and see what we could do to bring those forward. I'm pleased to announce that we're accelerating the realization of our cost program here in 2025 from what was $175 million to $225 million.
We completed the integration of our former Power Technologies segment into our aftermarket business into light vehicle and CV respectively. That's gone real well. Of the $300 million cost reduction, this integration is worth about $30 to 35 million of that. I think we're gonna see further benefits, not sort of SG&A-related benefits, as we leverage best practices across our aftermarket businesses. I think as we bring some of the operational rigor and processes that we have in light vehicle to Power Technologies, I see operational improvements flowing through in the back half of this year. More to come on that.
Lastly, in free cash flow, you know, Q1 is always a seasonal outflow, but we had a good start with, you know, despite lower revenues and profitability on an absolute basis. Our Q1 cash outflow was an improvement year-over-year of $67 million. We continue to focus on opportunities to reduce our CapEx, and I'm hoping that we can squeeze some money out of that in the back half of the year. You know, not that it's in free cash flow, but we are focused on a portfolio of non-core, non-strategic assets and things like that. We expect to deliver $50 million here in Q2 and could see our way maybe to another $50 million in the back half of the year. Generally, a good start to the year.
In terms of the outlook and what we're seeing, I guess I would start with a very dynamic situation, especially on the tariff front, you know, that changes significantly on a daily basis. Based on what we see right now, I guess I would just say our tariff situation is manageable. We can get into a lot more detail in some of the questions, but it's a manageable issue for Dana. Several mitigation actions have been completed. We've got recoveries into our customers with the right level of detail to support our claims being processed.
I guess the other thing I would note, if you look at the steel and aluminum tariffs. We've seen North America indices move up such that we expect we substantially recover the steel and aluminum through already negotiated mechanisms that we have in place with our customers. Could be some timing issues 'cause those tend to work in a little bit of a lag, but I would say the impact of steel and aluminum tariffs with the way the indices have moved would be kind of a non-issue for us as we see things right now. In terms of what we're seeing in the market, the first, I guess, thing what we are seeing is a reduction in schedules for our North American commercial vehicle customers.
You know, you see that in some of the calls that have come out before us, with people taking their assumptions for North America down. We've reflected that in our outlook. So that's sort of been a bit of a headwind for us. In off-highway, we're seeing a little bit of pre-buy interest here in Q2. Nothing significant, but it's nice to see we're getting a little bit of that. We are starting to see outside of North America some green shoots in terms of improvements in orders in the second half of the year. In North America, we aren't seeing anything in terms of LV schedules any deterioration at this point in time. If you look at the mix of vehicles that we're exposed to, it
You know, you guys all know where we've got, where our money is made. We feel pretty good about our customers gaining share in our, in our space. While we acknowledge there's some risk in the back half of the year, we're just being cautious right now. We don't see it reflecting up in our schedules. We talked earlier about the $50 million of incremental cost reduction. I guess I would just say, you know, absent tariffs, we'd be sitting here this morning raising our guidance by about $50 million to reflect the acceleration on the cost reduction side. We're just holding back until we get a little bit more clarity on what happens in LV, particularly in the second half.
Lastly, just a little bit of a something to brag about here, but we won our 10th PACE award. It's quite an honor in the industry. This for us is a hybrid transmission, which is kind of a niche product. It's about $25 million of sales this year. It's a product that we've rolled out across the highest end of the automotive spectrum, so customers like Aston Martin, Lamborghini, McLaren. We see this as a business opportunity to grow to $200, $250, maybe even up to $300 million over the next few years at a highly accretive EBITDA margin. This product pushes 20%.
Not a huge item, but it's an important, I think margin expansion arrow in our quiver, and I congratulate the technical team for winning the award. With that, Tim, I'll turn it over to you.
Timothy Kraus
SVP and CFO, Dana Inc
Thank you, Bruce, and good morning to everyone. If you'd please turn to slide eight for a review of our Q1 results. Sales were $2.4 billion, $383 million lower than last year, driven by lower demand across all of our end markets. Adjusted EBITDA was $188 million for a profit margin of 8%, just 20 basis points lower than last year on lower sales as the benefits of our cost improvement actions begin to take hold. Net income attributable to Dana was $25 million in Q1 2025, compared with $3 million last year. The difference was primarily due to the proposed divestiture of our non-core hydraulics business in 2024.
A $29 million loss was recorded to adjust the carrying value of net assets to fair value in last year's Q1. Income taxes for Q1 2025 were $29 million lower due to jurisdictional mix of profits and timing of payments. Finally, operating cash flow was a use, as is normally the case in Q1, of $37 million. This was an improvement of $65 million over Q1 last year due to lower working capital requirements. Please turn with me now to slide nine for the drivers of the sales and profit change. Beginning this quarter, we have revised our walk presentation to better detail the impacts of volume mix and performance of the operations. Previously, these two drivers were combined.
We continue to show the benefit of our cost-saving initiative, and we have added the actual impact of tariffs as part of our walk. Beginning with volume and mix on the left, we saw $345 million lower sales driven by lower demand in all of our end markets. Specifically, when compared to Q1 of last year, when light vehicle production increased dramatically coming off of the UAW strike at the end of 2023. This year, we are seeing a slowdown in production as vehicle inventories remain high. We did not see any distinct change in order patterns from our key customers, on key programs related to tariffs during the quarter. Adjusted EBITDA from sales volume and mix was lower by $90 million. This was a decremental margin of about 25%.
We are breaking out performance, which includes efficiency gains in our manufacturing, separately. Performance increased sales by $27 million, mostly through commercial actions, while profit increased by $35 million due to efficiency improvements across the company. For Q1 2025, cost-savings added $41 million in profit through the various actions we have taken. As Bruce mentioned, we have accelerated some actions. We now expect to realize about $50 million more of our $300 million in total cost-savings this year. To the left of the slide, we included a breakdown of where the permanent cost-savings are coming from. You can see it's well distributed across the cost structure. The tariff impact in the quarter was just $6 million.
Since our tariff recoveries will have a lag associated with them, we did not immediately recover the tariffs in the quarter, but we expect to receive recoveries throughout the year. Foreign currency translation decreased sales by $53 million, primarily driven by the lower value of the euro, real, and rupee compared to the US dollar. Profit was lower by $4 million with no impact to margin. Finally, commodity cost recoveries in the Q1 was $10 million lower than last year due to the timing of cost mechanisms within the co-commodity recovery agreements with our customers. Profit was $11 million lower as the prices fall through to profit. Next, I will turn to slide 10, the details of the Q1 adjusted free cash flow.
Adjusted free cash flow in Q1 2025 was a use of $101 million, which is $67 million higher than Q1 last year. Lower adjusted EBITDA and higher one-time costs related to the cost-saving actions and the sale of the off-highway business were offset by lower working capital requirements. Finally, capital spending, net of proceeds of sales of fixed assets, was about the same as last year. Please turn with me now to slide 11 for our guidance for 2025. Our 2025 Full Year guidance ranges remain unchanged. As a reminder, our guidance includes the off-highway business for the full year and includes the estimated impact of disclosed tariffs. First thing you will note is that we are expecting sales to be up above the midpoint of our range.
The higher sales expectations are taking into account some of the softening in commercial vehicle end markets, offset by the recovery of expected tariffs that will flow through sales, and the improved outlook on currency translation. To date, we've not seen a change in the volume expectations of our major light vehicle programs. Our initial expectations were for slightly weaker end-market demand for light trucks. If that market weakens further, we will adjust our outlook. Adjusted EBITDA is still expected to be $975 million at the midpoint of the range. This is approximately $90 million higher than 2024 and implies a profit margin of about 10%, a 140 basis points increase over 2024. Full year adjusted free cash flow is expected to be $225 million at the midpoint of the range for the year.
This is approximately $155 million higher than last year. Our adjusted EPS guidance is expected to be $1.40 per share at the midpoint of the range. This is down from our previous estimate solely due to the change in expected tax expense driven by our expected regional mix of profits. Lastly, please turn with me to slide 12 for an outlook of our adjusted free cash flow for 2025. We anticipate Full Year 2025 adjusted free cash flow to be about $225 million at the midpoint of the guidance range. We expect about $90 million of higher free cash flow from increased adjusted EBITDA. One-time costs will be about $20 million higher as we invest in our cost-savings program and we work to finalize the off-highway divestiture.
Working capital requirements will be about $50 million lower, and capital spending net is expected to be about $325 million this year, which is $45 million lower than 2024. Thank you, and I'll now ask Regina to open the call for questions.
Operator
At this time, if you would like to ask a question, press star then the number one on your telephone keypad. To ensure that everyone has an opportunity to participate in today's Q&A, we ask that callers limit themselves to one question at a time. If you'd like to ask an additional question, please return to the queue. Our first question comes from the line of Joseph Spak with UBS. Please go ahead.
Joseph Spak
Managing Director in Autos, Auto Suppliers and Auto-tech Equity Research Analyst, UBS
Thanks. Good morning, everyone. Maybe just to start on the guidance. I know you listed a number of things, you know, some tariff headwinds and some negative market assumptions, in what is, I guess, gonna be new Dana, but then cost-savings, and then you know, in off-highway business, you mentioned some of that pre-buy commentary. I guess the question is, you know, back in the beginning of the year, you provided some guidance for new Dana versus the off-highway. With all those factors you listed, is there any meaningful change to those assumptions we should consider?
Timothy Kraus
SVP and CFO, Dana Inc
Yeah. Commercial vehicles going to be a bit lower than what we had seen just a couple of months ago. That's largely being offset by amounts in light vehicle and in a little bit in off-highway. Obviously the balance of that is coming from what we believe will be additional revenue from tariff offsets.
R. Bruce McDonald
Chairman and CEO, Dana Inc
Yeah. I guess maybe just a couple other things, like obviously the incremental cost reduction target is all related to corporate, so, you know, gets sort of smeared based on sales. I would say, you know, in off-highway, you know, we are benefiting in our outlook, we are picking up some translation on the euro. That would be disproportionate to off-highway.
Timothy Kraus
SVP and CFO, Dana Inc
Correct.
R. Bruce McDonald
Chairman and CEO, Dana Inc
I mean, generally speaking, if you sort of, you know, $50 million cost reductions are pulled for, but if you think about when we gave sort of guidance around new Dana post off-highway sale in 2026, I think the message is look, Q1, you know, or new Dana is up year-over-year in margins, and off-highway is on a year-over-year basis down. The path to get new Dana in 2026 to the type of number that we commit to, the 10 to 10.5 is thoroughly on track.
Joseph Spak
Managing Director in Autos, Auto Suppliers and Auto-tech Equity Research Analyst, UBS
Okay. Just for 2025, again, I know you provided some ranges and it seems like some moving parts, but generally those ranges are still valid?
Timothy Kraus
SVP and CFO, Dana Inc
Yeah, they're generally valid. I mean, the sales are gonna move around as Bruce mentioned, right? Between tariffs and translation, we're gonna have some tailwind on the top line. That's largely going to offset the headwinds that we're seeing in commercial vehicle from a volume perspective.
R. Bruce McDonald
Chairman and CEO, Dana Inc
Yeah. I guess if you think about tariffs overall, you know, we don't bring in an awful lot of product from Europe into North America. When we talk about our tariff headwind, the off-highway impact is relatively small.
Joseph Spak
Managing Director in Autos, Auto Suppliers and Auto-tech Equity Research Analyst, UBS
Okay.
Timothy Kraus
SVP and CFO, Dana Inc
Yeah, that business is primarily European. We do have a bit of business here in North America. That's relatively small portion of the overall business.
Joseph Spak
Managing Director in Autos, Auto Suppliers and Auto-tech Equity Research Analyst, UBS
Okay. Bruce, appreciate you're limited in what you could say about the process. You know, I think you had some relatively encouraging commentary, but maybe you could just sort of indicate to us if sort of any of this market uncertainty has had any impact on the process, even in terms of sort of, you know, potential management distraction for potential buyers or anything there, or are things sort of mostly on track with what you thought?
R. Bruce McDonald
Chairman and CEO, Dana Inc
Yeah. I mean, I guess I would say obviously, you know, if you look at the last 90 days, I think the tariff situation is becoming clearer. You know, it was swinging around pretty wildly, when some of the IEPA stuff was coming up and the China thing was escalating and things like that. I think now some of the rules, we've had a little bit of stability. We're getting clarification in terms of what's in and out, how we handle USMCA, non-USMCA. I would say we've definitely had maximum uncertainty and, you know, in that environment, you know, people are nervous and wanna understand things. So spending a little bit more time with our teams.
I'd say, I mean, I really can't say a lot, but I guess we had sort of talked about being in a position to say something, come to a resolution here in early in Q2. Now, I guess I would just say that's our timing's probably more like late in Q2.
Joseph Spak
Managing Director in Autos, Auto Suppliers and Auto-tech Equity Research Analyst, UBS
Okay. Appreciate that.
R. Bruce McDonald
Chairman and CEO, Dana Inc
I mean, I wish I could say more, but the guys probably wanna yank me out of the room already, so.
Operator
Our next question comes from the line of Edison Yu with Deutsche Bank. Please go ahead.
Edison Yu
Director and Equity Analyst in Automotive and Electric Vehicle Sectors, Deutsche Bank
Hi, thank you for taking our questions. Just wanna come back on the tariff. Can you just share, I guess, what is the exposure at the moment? In terms of the timing of recovery, how long do you think that will take on average?
Timothy Kraus
SVP and CFO, Dana Inc
I don't wanna get into the overall exposure mostly because I don't really wanna negotiate, you know, with my customers in public. What I can say is from a recovery perspective, we expect it's probably going to be less than a quarter on a lag. Of course, that depends on the customer and the end market that we're dealing with. You know, most of our largest customers have set up a regimented process. As Bruce mentioned, we've already started to provide invoices and the detail backup that's required by our customers in order to obtain recovery.
That process is well underway and we see it working well given the level of detail that we're providing the customer. I'm guessing it's probably when they get through it. You know, obviously the customers are gonna be pretty inundated. We're looking at, you know, somewhere probably not longer than a quarter, but I think it'll end up being a little bit less given the impact that this will have across the supply base.
R. Bruce McDonald
Chairman and CEO, Dana Inc
Yeah. I mean, I'd expect it to be a cash flow timing issue in the quarter. I think by the time we're here in three months time, we will know what our recovery is and have that process nailed down sufficiently, so we'll be accruing the impact. The cash associated with it, like we have to pay that out much sooner than we're gonna get it back. I don't think that's gonna be a major bridge item for us, but I feel pretty comfortable that it's not gonna be a problem for us.
Edison Yu
Director and Equity Analyst in Automotive and Electric Vehicle Sectors, Deutsche Bank
In terms of the amount, is it yours or is it baked in that you would recover essentially 100%, or is there some like wiggle room or haircut to the recovery?
Timothy Kraus
SVP and CFO, Dana Inc
Our view is that we're going to be recovering 100% of the tariffs.
R. Bruce McDonald
Chairman and CEO, Dana Inc
Yeah. Yeah.
Edison Yu
Director and Equity Analyst in Automotive and Electric Vehicle Sectors, Deutsche Bank
Okay.
R. Bruce McDonald
Chairman and CEO, Dana Inc
I think maybe just to give a little bit of help there is first of all, if you think about our commercial vehicle business and our off-highway business, we have very little risk of a 100% recovery. That part of it, we're not worried about at all. I mentioned that the aluminum and steel will be recovered through normal indices that we already have in place. Once you sort of back out those three things and some mitigation actions that we've taken where we were the importer of record of finished goods, like we bring some axles up from Mexico to North America, and they're picked up at a warehouse in Laredo. We've renegotiated those exposures away.
Now you're left with a fairly minor amount in the scheme of the 10 billion dollar company. We have all the documentation submitted to our light vehicle customers, and they've brought in external resource to process our claims. In one case, we know our claim has been processed and approved, but I haven't seen the check yet. We'll see where we end up.
Edison Yu
Director and Equity Analyst in Automotive and Electric Vehicle Sectors, Deutsche Bank
Understood. Just one last thing to clarify. I really am not quantifying the exposure, you know, but in terms of the mechanics, is it basically the non-USMCA part that you're assuming gets exempt, or are you assuming that there's more than that or the USMCA actually goes away?
Timothy Kraus
SVP and CFO, Dana Inc
Well, what we've put out in terms of our guidance now is based on what we see coming out of Washington as of today. That will change tomorrow, I have no doubt. It changed last night. But you know, with the way that the mechanisms are working with our customers, that we need to be able to prove the actual amount of tariffs that we've incurred and be able to trace them back by part number. That's the documentation that we're providing. You know, our expectation is that level of detail will allow us to recover the tariffs from our customers.
R. Bruce McDonald
Chairman and CEO, Dana Inc
It's a little bit more nuanced than your question. Let me just give you an example. Everything that we're talking about is for auto parts. It does not include our parts the way the definition in the HTS.
Timothy Kraus
SVP and CFO, Dana Inc
HTS
R. Bruce McDonald
Chairman and CEO, Dana Inc
... HTS codes are written. It does not include things like our off-highway and commercial vehicle products, nor does it even include some of our Super Duty business. They aren't in this whole Section 232 switch that happened yesterday. They're still in the other buckets, IEPA, reciprocals, things like that.
Edison Yu
Director and Equity Analyst in Automotive and Electric Vehicle Sectors, Deutsche Bank
Gotcha. Very much appreciated. Thank you.
R. Bruce McDonald
Chairman and CEO, Dana Inc
Yeah. Yeah.
Operator
Our next question comes from the line of Colin Langan with Wells Fargo. Please go ahead.
Colin Langan
Automotive & Mobility Analyst, Wells Fargo Securities
Oh, great. Thanks for taking my questions. Any way to frame what you're assuming for light vehicle production, is it very in line with the recent S&P forecast? Yeah, is there any way to frame that? Because, you know, obviously a lot of uncertainty with tariffs.
R. Bruce McDonald
Chairman and CEO, Dana Inc
Sure.
Timothy Kraus
SVP and CFO, Dana Inc
Yeah. I think the way, like, you know, obviously, you know, when you think about the light vehicle outlook, we try to steer everybody back to the light truck production. We currently aren't seeing any substantial change from where we were when we came out in February. That's what's currently baked into our forecast for North American light truck. If that changes in any material way, we'll have to revisit, you know, our outlook. Right now, we haven't seen anything and don't have anything from our customers on the horizon. That doesn't mean it won't change, but at this point, that's currently. We're looking at it largely the same as we did two months ago.
R. Bruce McDonald
Chairman and CEO, Dana Inc
The only thing I'd add to that, Colin, is you know, we acknowledge there's a risk there, and that's why we're not up in our guide.
Colin Langan
Automotive & Mobility Analyst, Wells Fargo Securities
Got it. On the S&P side, I mean, is it consistent with what S&P just provided or more optimistic, less optimistic?
R. Bruce McDonald
Chairman and CEO, Dana Inc
I would say the latest S&P data which there's we don't think is accurate, especially here in the short-term in some of it. If you looked at the latest S&P information and we were to factor that in, we'd have more than enough coverage in the extra cost save to hold our guide.
Colin Langan
Automotive & Mobility Analyst, Wells Fargo Securities
Got it. That's helpful. You know, if I look at, I think you said earlier, you didn't wanna provide like a number on the tariff impact. I mean, in the EBIT walk, it's $6 million. I mean, is that not a runway we should think about for a long point?
Timothy Kraus
SVP and CFO, Dana Inc
Well, you have to, I mean, the tariffs were not for the entire quarter. They were staged in. You know, you can't use the Q1 as sort of a viewpoint for the tariffs. They've also changed, you know.
R. Bruce McDonald
Chairman and CEO, Dana Inc
Yeah
Timothy Kraus
SVP and CFO, Dana Inc
From week-to-week. Depending on when we imported the material and how it was classified determines what the impact was in the quarter. That's going to be different going forward. You cannot use the Q1 and try to
R. Bruce McDonald
Chairman and CEO, Dana Inc
Yeah
Timothy Kraus
SVP and CFO, Dana Inc
do some sort of extrapolation. The rules and how these things are classified have changed dramatically from week-to-week.
R. Bruce McDonald
Chairman and CEO, Dana Inc
The $4 million of the $6 million, Colin, is related to where Dana was the importer of record, the example I gave in the previous call. We've already remediated that and built it, and we're not at all worried about getting that $4 million back. But yeah, like Tim said, there's things that have come on and come off. There's bucketing issues, except there's HTS code issues, et cetera.
Timothy Kraus
SVP and CFO, Dana Inc
Yeah. You have to remember, right, like, a lot of this stuff is coming out in either an executive order or in a press release or a press conference. It then gets published in the commercial register, and then that's translated by the Commerce Department into and at the U.S. Customs and Border Protection to determine how and what HTS codes are gonna collect what tariffs on which. It is, you know, exceedingly complex and is changing as, you know, both the rules get more clarification and the rules change.
R. Bruce McDonald
Chairman and CEO, Dana Inc
Maybe just to like say a few sort of, you know, scene setters on it, to maybe kind of get your understanding a bit better. Overall, our flow of goods from Mexico back up here to the United States is $700 to 800 million, and our Canada flow of goods is, like, $100 million. You know, that split, 55% is USMCA compliant. Some of that also doesn't have anything to do with its Section 232 because it relates-
Timothy Kraus
SVP and CFO, Dana Inc
No
R. Bruce McDonald
Chairman and CEO, Dana Inc
... to our commercial vehicle business. Our other exposure that we have is reciprocal tariffs on castings and things like that we, like everybody else, buy from Korea and particularly India. Those are, you know, the headlines of where our exposures come from and kind of magnitude.
Timothy Kraus
SVP and CFO, Dana Inc
Yeah. I'll also point out that some of the material that's coming in that's non-USMCA compliant is directly sourced by the customer. We don't have a choice on where we're bringing in some of the parts based on the customer requirements. Again, that is.
R. Bruce McDonald
Chairman and CEO, Dana Inc
Yeah
Timothy Kraus
SVP and CFO, Dana Inc
you know, recovered dollar one right away because, you know, we don't have any choice.
R. Bruce McDonald
Chairman and CEO, Dana Inc
Yeah.
Colin Langan
Automotive & Mobility Analyst, Wells Fargo Securities
You said $700 to 800 million Mexico, $100 million Canada. Any number on what's from the rest of the world brought into the United States?
Timothy Kraus
SVP and CFO, Dana Inc
Yeah, we're talking, you know, $a few hundred million more. I mean, it obviously depends on production and where we're at. Largely those sorts of numbers.
Colin Langan
Automotive & Mobility Analyst, Wells Fargo Securities
Got it. All right. Thank you very much. That's my question.
R. Bruce McDonald
Chairman and CEO, Dana Inc
Thank you.
Operator
Our next question comes from the line of James Picariello with BNP Paribas. Please go ahead.
James Picariello
Director and Head U.S. Autos Research, BNP Paribas
Hey, good morning, everybody. Just as we think about the off-highway sale and if we just consider the tariff exposure for the off-highway business. We know off-highway, as was mentioned, right, does not fall under Section 232 autos tariffs, right? It would be subject to the broader Liberation Day tariffs. That's a question just to confirm. Just regarding off-highway's regional sales mix, right, we know about 65% of total sales get produced in Europe. Can you just size up what portion of that, you know, properly constitutes North America US sales for off-highway, and what portion gets imported to understand the trade flow there? Thanks.
Timothy Kraus
SVP and CFO, Dana Inc
You know, North America is a few hundred million dollars. A portion of that gets imported. It's. I mean, I'd have to go look at the specifics, and we can get you that. Overall, US tariff exposure for off-highway is very small and is 100% recoverable from the customer. You know, we've already proactively actioned those with those customers to get recovery. It's. The tariff impact is not the issue around off-highway.
I think the broader issue, and this is true for tariff generally, is, hey, how does this affect the macroeconomic environment and how might it affect volume, you know, in all the end markets at the end of the day? That and especially for off-highway, that's probably the bigger issue, right? As they pass these things through, how is it gonna affect the various end markets within off-highway? To date, we're not seeing-
James Picariello
Director and Head U.S. Autos Research, BNP Paribas
All right.
Timothy Kraus
SVP and CFO, Dana Inc
We haven't seen anything, and we've seen a little bit of pre-buy. You know, when we look out at the back half of the year, we are starting to see the green shoots we were expecting. Right now, you know, things are holding up pretty well. You know, it's a pretty fluid situation, and you know, we're monitoring it pretty closely.
James Picariello
Director and Head U.S. Autos Research, BNP Paribas
That's really helpful. Just my follow-up. I know it's a sensitive question, sensitive answer. Previous timing of the off-highway sale did point to, like, something around Q2. Just curious if you have, you know, if you could share any thoughts there. Just within the revenue guidance. You know, two things that are not tied to tariffs, right? FX and commodities in your revenue. Can you just confirm what those guidance assumptions, those guidance updates are? Thanks.
Timothy Kraus
SVP and CFO, Dana Inc
I'm not gonna provide the update 'cause then you can sort of back into what our tariff assumptions are. They're you know, in terms of commodities, we would expect to be up a little bit and obviously the FX is gonna be an additional tailwind. I don't wanna get into specifics. We'll obviously be able to show that to you when we bring out Q2 on the off-highway sales as Bruce mentioned earlier. You know, we were expecting early to mid-Q2 given the amount of work that's being done by the bidders.
We would expect that to move a little bit and probably be, you know, later in the Q2.
James Picariello
Director and Head U.S. Autos Research, BNP Paribas
Thank you.
Operator
Our next question comes from the line of Ryan Brinkman with J.P. Morgan. Please go ahead.
Ryan Brinkman
Lead Automotive Equity Research Analyst and Head of U.S. Autos and Auto Parts, J.P. Morgan
Hi. Thanks for taking my question, which is in regard to the cost-savings, including after, you know, following the acceleration this quarter, the $225 million you're looking for this year, it's now up to 25% of last year's EBITDA. That's really just a huge step change in cost. I wanted to check in, again on the source of those savings, including the incremental savings. I think I heard you say largely corporate in nature. Also your confidence in the ability to achieve the savings. Last quarter you were very confident. And then finally, you know, just like whether the costs are sustainable or don't have any associated drawbacks. For example, are you mostly cutting through corporate bureaucracy or layers of management, discretionary, but not R&D?
I'm asking only because the magnitude of savings is so impressive that it sort of begs the question of like, if there really was all this fat to cut, you know, why had it maybe not been targeted before?
Timothy Kraus
SVP and CFO, Dana Inc
Thanks, Ryan. That's a lot. I'll try to unpack it in some reasonable manner. I'll take the one that I like the most. In terms of our confidence, we are absolutely confident that we will, one, deliver the 225, and two, deliver the $300 million on a run rate basis. If you just look at Q1, right? It's $41 million of incremental savings. We had $10 million of savings in Q4. If you just take that's $51 million. Multiply that by four, that's 200 of the 225 when you think about it, right? On a run rate basis already. We took costs out all through Q1.
Our run rate action number is already trending to where we need to be to deliver the $225 million. We've got additional actions to happen throughout the year, but we are in very, very good shape to deliver the $225 million. We wouldn't be here telling you we're gonna deliver the $225 million if we weren't absolutely positive we're gonna deliver it. To give you some idea, and we broke out a little bit on the slide, you know, sort of the percentages, but the really big buckets that, if you wanna think about the $300 million, 70% of that number is coming from headcount and engineering, alone. An additional about 10% is related to the consolidation actions around the segments.
If you just get through that's 80% of the number in those buckets. If we look at the headcount, we've actioned over 70% of the headcount that we have slated to reduce within the organization has already been actioned. The balance of that will be done through the rest of the year with a large chunk of that coming out late in Q2. We have visibility to where these costs are coming out and what's driving and our ability to deliver them. When you think about it, you know, what's really, you know, to get your question, "Hey, was there a lot of fat?
What was it?" Well, if you think about engineering and even some of the headcount, a lot of that's related to the change in how we're addressing the EV business and where we think we need to be sized for where the EV business is today and where it's likely to go. So it's a big part of that cost reduction is coming from the shift in strategy and expectation around our EV business.
The balance is, yeah, we're, you know, we took a really hard look at what we need to run the business and how we can get better at how we're running the business, especially around the corporate and overhead functions, whether they be, you know, physically here at corporate or in the business units themselves.
Ryan Brinkman
Lead Automotive Equity Research Analyst and Head of U.S. Autos and Auto Parts, J.P. Morgan
Very helpful. Thank you. Just maybe on the segmentation change. I see also with the Power Technologies being absorbed into the various different, you know, driveline, motion segments. Previously you'd contemplated, and I think you've been moving away from that already because of the growing importance of Power Technologies and, you know, thermal regulation for electrification, et cetera. But does this kind of definitively kind of close the door on that, or does it sort of reflect how you go to market? What was some of the thought process behind that?
Timothy Kraus
SVP and CFO, Dana Inc
Yeah. It definitely closes the door on it. Power Technologies is not for sale. It’s a good business and it was really just a reflection of we think we can run leaner by having one less segment. Like I mentioned earlier, that alone is worth $35 million in terms of doing the consolidation. I expect-
R. Bruce McDonald
Chairman and CEO, Dana Inc
That we will get further improvement, not SG&A, so we won't be counting it in our $300 million. I do expect we're gonna see significant opportunities to drive our margins as we leverage best practices across aftermarket, and we bring in some of the rigor that we have in light vehicle that was not as strong in our Power Technologies operations.
Ryan Brinkman
Lead Automotive Equity Research Analyst and Head of U.S. Autos and Auto Parts, J.P. Morgan
Very helpful. Thank you.
R. Bruce McDonald
Chairman and CEO, Dana Inc
All right. Thanks.
Timothy Kraus
SVP and CFO, Dana Inc
Thanks, Ryan.
Operator
Our next question comes from the line of Dan Levy with Barclays. Please go ahead.
Dan Levy
Senior Equity Research Analyst of Autos and Mobility, Barclays
Hi. Good morning. Thanks for taking the questions. Bruce, in your prepared remarks, you mentioned some actions around non-core assets and getting some proceeds in Q2, another $50 million in the back half of the year.
R. Bruce McDonald
Chairman and CEO, Dana Inc
Mm-hmm.
Dan Levy
Senior Equity Research Analyst of Autos and Mobility, Barclays
Could you maybe just talk about what some of those assets are, and maybe?
R. Bruce McDonald
Chairman and CEO, Dana Inc
Sure
Dan Levy
Senior Equity Research Analyst of Autos and Mobility, Barclays
... how deep is the set of assets out there that you view to be non-core at Dana?
R. Bruce McDonald
Chairman and CEO, Dana Inc
Yeah. I'll let Tim take it on. I mean, you know, this is really, you know, with me coming in saying, "Hey, what are some bits and pieces of non-core minority JVs, et cetera, surplus assets, land, you know, those types of things?" There's not a lot. I wouldn't say there's hundreds of millions, but you know, there's lots of things, $1, $2, $5 million that we can auction a couple in the $30, $40 million range. Go ahead and give a
Timothy Kraus
SVP and CFO, Dana Inc
Yeah. I'll just give you the best example. We, you know, had a non-consolidated joint venture in India that was in the commercial vehicle space. We own 48% of the business. It's non-core. It's a supplier both to us and to others. We sold that in Q2 for over $40 million. That, you know, is an asset that is sitting on the books at a far lower value than that and doesn't change anything related to how we run the business.
I think you know those types of assets, and you know, we have a handful of those types of things where you know when we you know if you go back over time we felt it was important to have equity interests in some of these types of operations. We don't think that that's true anymore. Some of that's just because, hey, these joint ventures have grown and matured, and we don't need to be that close to them. Valuations in some of these places are pretty high, and so we're using the opportunity to divest them.
You know, to the extent they're a supplier, put a supply agreement in that gives us preferential supply, and then take the capital and redeploy it into something that has a far better return from our perspective.
R. Bruce McDonald
Chairman and CEO, Dana Inc
Yeah. Just like, you know, our dividends from that joint venture are less than $1 million a year. Like Tim said, we've got, I think it was just in the low 40s pre-tax.
Timothy Kraus
SVP and CFO, Dana Inc
Yeah
R. Bruce McDonald
Chairman and CEO, Dana Inc
earlier this week. It's just looking at things like that.
Dan Levy
Senior Equity Research Analyst of Autos and Mobility, Barclays
Oh, okay. Thank you. As a follow-up, Tim, you'd mentioned that obviously a piece of the cost-savings relates to EVs and, you know, maybe changes in the program schedules. You know, we actually haven't even seen yet any true modifications to OEM plans.
R. Bruce McDonald
Chairman and CEO, Dana Inc
Yeah
Dan Levy
Senior Equity Research Analyst of Autos and Mobility, Barclays
Understand that some of this is maybe proactive, but wondering if the cancellations or delays or shifts start to come in, is there maybe further opportunity to pull back on some of the EV side?
R. Bruce McDonald
Chairman and CEO, Dana Inc
Yeah. I'll take that one.
Dan Levy
Senior Equity Research Analyst of Autos and Mobility, Barclays
Because I believe that EV is a small piece. Yeah, thank you.
R. Bruce McDonald
Chairman and CEO, Dana Inc
Yeah, I'll take that one, here. It's not really what you just said. It is when we changed our strategy, what we said was where you know we have ICE business and EV, you know, we wanna be a partner's technology of choice, and therefore we're willing to invest our capital and our engineering to chase that type of business and but making sure we get the right level of risk-sharing.
Where we don't have any ICE business and we're chasing incremental volumes, or we're dealing with customers where we're in the next generation investment and the first generation that has volumes are 5 or 10% of what we thought, we are saying it needs to be 100% funded, otherwise we're just not willing to bear the risk. It's more a question of us lowering our pursuit of new electric business to reflect the massive increase in risk.
Timothy Kraus
SVP and CFO, Dana Inc
Yeah. I think it's that, and then, you know, our engineering is always shown net, right? You know, to the extent programs are continuing, so they haven't been canceled, but now instead of us outflowing the engineering dollars, you know, the customer is responsible for that on a pay-as-you-go basis.
R. Bruce McDonald
Chairman and CEO, Dana Inc
And-
Timothy Kraus
SVP and CFO, Dana Inc
That's some of it. There is a big chunk where we had a lot of development plans where we were developing products and technologies that, you know, given the slowdown in the market, we don't need to create the second, third or, you know, the third generation of a product today. Our customers are more than happy to continue to use the first or the second generation of those products for a much longer period of time. That's allowed us to reduce the amount of engineering dollars we have to spend on those next gen programs.
R. Bruce McDonald
Chairman and CEO, Dana Inc
I guess the kind of your question and where you're going is, as our customers look at their product plans, 'cause I'm sure they're leaving no stone unturned in terms of what actions they can take to mitigate the impact of tariffs. I'm sure looking at some of their EV pipeline is going to be on the table. To the extent they decide to push some programs, I would say there's one or two that could, if they were to push them out, would have a favorable impact on mainly our capital, but it wouldn't be a 2025 savings. It would be a 2026 and 2027 type number that would come down.
Dan Levy
Senior Equity Research Analyst of Autos and Mobility, Barclays
Great. Thank you. Very helpful.
Operator
Our next question comes from the line of Emmanuel Rosner with Wolfe Research. Please go ahead.
Emmanuel Rosner
Senior Autos & Auto Technology Analyst, Wolfe Research
Thank you. Good morning. I was hoping you can help us with how to think about cadence of, you know, revenue and earnings for the rest of the year. What's assumed in your reiterated guidance, and in particular, sort of like, you know, back half versus first half?
Timothy Kraus
SVP and CFO, Dana Inc
Yeah, I mean, largely, the same as we talked about, Emmanuel, a couple of months ago. We do expect the first half to be weaker. Q1 to be the weakest, and then we would expect to see, again, under our current volume assumptions, to see a recovery in the back half of the year. That's still our expectation for revenue.
R. Bruce McDonald
Chairman and CEO, Dana Inc
I guess as we go out, though, the sort of headwind that we saw in revenue starts to decline sequentially.
Timothy Kraus
SVP and CFO, Dana Inc
Correct.
Emmanuel Rosner
Senior Autos & Auto Technology Analyst, Wolfe Research
Okay. That's a volume assumption around the back half. I guess in terms of the headwind you're describing, you're talking about some of the destocking?
R. Bruce McDonald
Chairman and CEO, Dana Inc
Yeah. It's not so much.
Emmanuel Rosner
Senior Autos & Auto Technology Analyst, Wolfe Research
Yeah.
R. Bruce McDonald
Chairman and CEO, Dana Inc
It's not so much of our volume assumption. It's we're going against easier comps.
Emmanuel Rosner
Senior Autos & Auto Technology Analyst, Wolfe Research
Yeah.
R. Bruce McDonald
Chairman and CEO, Dana Inc
If you think about
Emmanuel Rosner
Senior Autos & Auto Technology Analyst, Wolfe Research
Right
R. Bruce McDonald
Chairman and CEO, Dana Inc
Q1 of last year, volumes were up because the customers were rebuilding from the strike. We had off-highway, you know, hadn't sort of started to slow down. As we go through getting to Q2, there's less of a year-over-year headwind on off-highway, and on LV. Same thing on LV. When, you know, this quarter we're down $300-something million, that delta drops sequentially quarter-over-quarter here.
Timothy Kraus
SVP and CFO, Dana Inc
Yeah, exactly. I mean, the big drivers, you know, when we were having this conversation a couple months ago were really around light vehicle and off-highway. You know, we're seeing a little bit of additional weakness from a CV perspective, but that's more than being offset by, from a top line anyway, from tariffs and our expected gains on the FX, assuming the FX stays kind of where it's where we're seeing today, especially around the euro.
Emmanuel Rosner
Senior Autos & Auto Technology Analyst, Wolfe Research
Got it. On the tariff side, it's obviously encouraging to see that you expect to recover, you know, everything from your customers. Have there been some discussions with them around longer-term moves that will be needed to address?
R. Bruce McDonald
Chairman and CEO, Dana Inc
Yeah
Emmanuel Rosner
Senior Autos & Auto Technology Analyst, Wolfe Research
some of, you know, where the capacity is?
R. Bruce McDonald
Chairman and CEO, Dana Inc
That's-
Emmanuel Rosner
Senior Autos & Auto Technology Analyst, Wolfe Research
Will there be need for reshoring? Do you need to move anything?
R. Bruce McDonald
Chairman and CEO, Dana Inc
Yeah. I mean, it's a good question, and what I would tell you is there's been so much volatility in what the rules are that as an industry, we have not had enough time to know what the rule is to start to do exactly what you just said. I think right now, you know, some of the information that came out last night, you know, we'll have to sift through that. We're definitely now in a position, and we're having early discussions about what are the types of things that we can do to mitigate the issue from either reshoring or changing some suppliers, flipping things that aren't USMCA compliant, et cetera.
What is 100% clear, though, is there's some things that if you take a two-year window, are not gonna be addressed. Just use castings as an example. Everybody buys castings from India. In the next two years, we're not going to be in a position where we can reshore that. You know, they're subject to the 10% reciprocals right now. You know, before there was a higher list of additional reciprocal tariffs, so we're just gonna have to wait and see how those play out as the administration negotiates some of these trade deals. Hey, we're running against our time, so I'm gonna have to wrap it up right now. Do we have one more question?
Emmanuel Rosner
Senior Autos & Auto Technology Analyst, Wolfe Research
There's one.
R. Bruce McDonald
Chairman and CEO, Dana Inc
Oh, I'm sorry.
Operator
Yeah. We'll take our final question from the line of Douglas Karson at Bank of America. Please go ahead.
Douglas Karson
Managing Director in Fixed Income Research, Bank of America
Great, guys. Thanks for letting me in the last question here. I really appreciate it. You know, bondholders have been pretty excited about the future of debt reduction and leverage coming down. I know we can't talk about the sale of off-highway. Could just refresh us or just reconfirm that your balance sheet de-levering is still a focus, and we could see a meaningful reduction in debt. Is that still the game plan?
Timothy Kraus
SVP and CFO, Dana Inc
That is. Absolutely.
Douglas Karson
Managing Director in Fixed Income Research, Bank of America
All right. That's helpful for us. I think the last target we had was leverage being in the, like, the one to two turn kind of range through the cycle. I'm not gonna pin you down on that, but is that still kind of directionally where we're headed?
Timothy Kraus
SVP and CFO, Dana Inc
Yeah. We've been talking about sort of one turn through the cycle on a net basis.
Douglas Karson
Managing Director in Fixed Income Research, Bank of America
Net basis. Okay. All right. That's good news.
Timothy Kraus
SVP and CFO, Dana Inc
Again, through the cycle, so you know, at different points, it might be a little lower, at different points, it might be higher. But on a net basis, one turn.
R. Bruce McDonald
Chairman and CEO, Dana Inc
Yeah.
Douglas Karson
Managing Director in Fixed Income Research, Bank of America
Great.
R. Bruce McDonald
Chairman and CEO, Dana Inc
I mean, again, just to help, you know, we believe that upon the sale of off-highway, we'd be required to tender our bonds.
Timothy Kraus
SVP and CFO, Dana Inc
Yeah.
Douglas Karson
Managing Director in Fixed Income Research, Bank of America
Okay. Helpful. Thank you.
R. Bruce McDonald
Chairman and CEO, Dana Inc
Okay. All right. Maybe with that, I'll just, you know, first of all, obviously, a big thank you to the Dana global team. I mean, we have a lot going on, and tariffs was something that we certainly weren't thinking was gonna get thrown at us three months ago. I just couldn't be prouder of the results our teams have delivered in the environment that we're in here. You know, we feel really good about the things that we have control on. We're 100% certain on our cost reduction savings that we can bring those forward. I think from an overall point of view, the things that we can control and manage, our teams are doing a great job. We look forward to sharing further progress on things in 90 days.
Thank you, everybody.
Timothy Kraus
SVP and CFO, Dana Inc
Thanks, guys.
Operator
This will conclude today's meeting. Thank you all for joining. You may now disconnect.

Operator
Good morning, and welcome to Dana Incorporated's Q4 and full year 2024 financial webcast and conference call. My name is Regina, and I will be your conference facilitator. Please be advised that our meeting today, both the speaker's remarks and Q&A session, will be recorded for replay purposes. For those participants who would like to access the call from the webcast, please reference the URL on our website and sign in as a guest. There will be a question and answer period after the speaker's remarks, and we will take questions from the telephone only. To ensure that everyone has an opportunity to participate in today's Q&A, we ask that callers limit themselves to one question at a time. If you would like to ask an additional question, please return to the queue.
At this time, I would like to begin the presentation by turning the call over to Dana's Senior Director of Investor Relations, Strategic Planning and Corporate Communications, Craig Barber. Please go ahead, Mr. Barber.
Craig Barber
Senior Director of Investor Relations, Strategic Planning, and Corporate Communication, Dana Incorporated
Good morning, everyone, and thanks for joining us today for Dana Incorporated's 2024 Q4 and full year earnings call. Today's presentation includes forward-looking statements about our expectations for Dana's future performance. Actual results could differ from what we've discussed today. For more details about the factors that could affect our future results, please refer to our safe harbor statement found in our public filings and our reports with the SEC. You'll find this morning's press release and presentation on our investor website. As a reminder, today's call is being recorded and the supporting materials are the property of Dana Incorporated. They may not be recorded, copied, or rebroadcast without our written consent. On this call this morning is Bruce McDonald, Dana Chairman and Chief Executive Officer, and Timothy Kraus, Senior Vice President and Chief Financial Officer.
Now I'd like to turn the call over to Bruce to get us started.
Bruce McDonald
Chairman and CEO, Dana Incorporated

If you were to hold FX, commodity, and volume constant, you know, across the three-year period, you should be able to just you will just add the amounts in the backlog to our sales to get what our resulting sales would be in 2025, 2026, 2027. You know, the idea that, hey, there's gonna be a lot more volume on our current programs, that would not be in our backlog. It would be in our market outlook. But it won't.
Now, if they bring out a brand-new variant or something like that would go to backlog, something we haven't previously made, or sold to the automakers, but not pure volume.
Dan Levy
Senior Equity Research Analyst of Autos and Mobility, Barclays
Great. Okay. Thank you. Just as a follow-up, with the news of potential tariffs on steel and aluminum, can you just remind us of how this played out when we saw this in 2018, and just what the timing effects are of you passing this on to your customers?
Timothy Kraus
SVP and CFO, Dana Incorporated
Yeah. You know, I know this came up a little bit earlier. What we, you know, we've obviously looking at the impacts are likely to be on the business, and we continue to kind of work through that. As we know more about, like, how they're gonna deal with, you know, materials and some of the other nuances within the supply chain, we'll know more. One thing we have done is we have put all of our customers on formal notice. We formally notify them that it is our intention to pass through every dollar of tariff that comes through as a result of it, and that we expect them that they're going to pay.
Bruce McDonald
Chairman and CEO, Dana Incorporated
Yeah. I guess I'd maybe add to that, Dan, is if you think about the light vehicle business, we're far more indexed now than we would have been back then. To the extent the tariffs drive up the cost, the recovery mechanism through indexes we already have in place is higher than it was back in 2018.
Timothy Kraus
SVP and CFO, Dana Incorporated
Yeah. That at least gets you 75%. Our view is we're not gonna eat the-
Bruce McDonald
Chairman and CEO, Dana Incorporated
The 25%
Timothy Kraus
SVP and CFO, Dana Incorporated
... the 25% that doesn't get recovered in our current commodity agreements.
Bruce McDonald
Chairman and CEO, Dana Incorporated
Correct.
Timothy Kraus
SVP and CFO, Dana Incorporated
We also don't know if it'll be reflected in the indexes or not. It may be surcharged. We just don't know. At the end of the day, our intention and our expectation is that our customers will pay every dollar.
Dan Levy
Senior Equity Research Analyst of Autos and Mobility, Barclays
All right. Thank you.
Timothy Kraus
SVP and CFO, Dana Incorporated
Yep.
Bruce McDonald
Chairman and CEO, Dana Incorporated
Okay. Maybe just in a few concluding remarks, I guess, first of all, I'd like to thank the Dana team and our leaders for delivering our improved financial results. You know, for me personally, I feel really good about the progress the team is making in actioning the $300 million cost reduction roadmap that we have. 2025 for us is gonna be a transformational year for Dana. The sale of our Off-Highway business is gonna unlock significant shareholder value, while at the same time enabling us to return capital to our shareholders and be left with a best-in-class balance sheet in our space. I'm really excited to be here, and I look forward to sharing our progress in three months' time. Thank you, everyone.
Operator
That will conclude today's call. Thank you all for joining. You may now disconnect.
